clue.text: You may well find a course arranged on it

definitions.text: You may well find a course arranged on it

parts.words: You may well find a course arranged on it
parts.note: reads like a racecourse or golf course laid out, but the course is a dish of a meal set down on a small table mat

explanation.surface: Someone wonders where a race or golf course might be laid out.
explanation.definitionFit: A table mat under each diner's plate is where a course of the meal is set down.

clue.text: Country hotels unfortunately having nothing as an extra

indicators.note: things going unfortunately go awry, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A country's hotels are sadly empty, with nothing extra on offer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges HOTELS to LESOTH, and O (nothing) is tacked on 'as an extra' at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, an example of a country.

clue.text: Emperor's son adopting a course?

parts.note: Caesar was the title of the Roman emperors; with the possessive it gives CAESARS
a son is a lad, a boy

explanation.surface: An emperor's boy is taking up a course of study.
explanation.walkthrough: The son (LAD) 'adopting' A takes it on in front of him. 'course' looks like a study course but is a dish of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: This salad of romaine, croutons and parmesan is served as one course of a meal.

clue.text: Join in expression of surprise once

definitions.meaning: to join two people in wedlock
an old exclamation of surprise or indignation, short for 'by Mary'

explanation.surface: A request to join in an old-fashioned cry of surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' simply links the two definitions; 'once' marks the exclamation as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: To wed a couple is to join them, and the archaic oath 'by Mary' was shortened to this exclamation.

clue.text: Hurry up with a German exchange deal?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: to hurry is to dart
ein is German for a

explanation.surface: Someone urges a German to hurry up with a trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the hurry word in this down clue, giving TRAD; the question mark flags that 'exchange deal' is a loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Handing over an old item as part payment for a new one is a part-exchange arrangement.

clue.text: Little power in market after I pass on information

indicators.note: the market piece comes after the letter I, so I leads the answer
the little power letter is placed inside the market word

parts.note: a mart is a market
P is the short form of power in physics

explanation.surface: Someone passes on information about a weak force in the marketplace.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart knowledge is to communicate it, to pass it on to another person.

clue.text: Rude about King? That's unwise

indicators.note: the rude word goes around the king's letter, enclosing it

parts.note: impudent means rude, cheeky
R is short for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Being rude about the monarch is not a sensible move.
explanation.walkthrough: IMPUDENT goes 'about' R, giving IMP-R-UDENT. 'That's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Imprudent is a direct synonym of unwise: lacking care or good judgement.

clue.text: Greek character set up one way to pay

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the pieces are read upwards, backwards

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
HP is hire purchase, buying in instalments

explanation.surface: A Greek is setting up a method of payment.
explanation.walkthrough: I and HP, read upwards under 'set up', give the letters reversed. HP (hire purchase) is the British term for buying on instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: Phi is the twenty-first letter of the Greek alphabet, so a Greek character.

clue.text: Author tried jogging?

definitions.meaning: Arthur ..., English writer of Swallows and Amazons
a whimsical reading: having a go at jogging

explanation.surface: A writer has taken up running.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as RAN SOME, the author's name describes someone who tried a little running.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome was the English writer of the Swallows and Amazons children's books.

clue.text: Scream "MP again misbehaving, as part of this?

definitions.text: Scream "MP again misbehaving, as part of this?

indicators.note: letters that misbehave are out of order, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: A headline-style cry of 'MP misbehaving again' is part of a political mudslinging effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misbehaving' rearranges SCREAM, MP and AGAIN; the whole clue is also an example of what the answer is.
explanation.definitionFit: A coordinated effort to damage a reputation with allegations, such as shouting about an MP's misbehaviour.

clue.text: Group in second year displaying risqué behaviour?

indicators.note: the group word sits inside the letters for second and year

parts.note: a team is a group

explanation.surface: A second-year group is behaving a little raunchily.
explanation.definitionFit: Steamy describes something erotic or racy, as risqué behaviour is.

clue.text: Paint bird and cat without first trace of style

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless bird

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the cat goes around the letter

parts.note: a lion is a big cat

indicators.note: the first trace of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone paints a bird and a cat with no sense of style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking: the cat surrounds the first letter of 'style'.
explanation.definitionFit: Emulsion is a water-based paint used on walls and ceilings.

clue.text: Concert is rearranged by the French rock venue?

indicators.note: rearranged means the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: A concert is reorganised by French promoters at a rock venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rearranged' scrambles the first two words into STONECIRC; 'by' just places the French article after them.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring of standing stones like Stonehenge is a site of rock, playfully a venue.

clue.text: Against intellectual study as a matter of principle

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
science is systematic intellectual study

explanation.surface: Someone opposes academic study on principle.
explanation.definitionFit: One's inner moral sense decides what is right, so it governs matters of principle.

clue.text: List of places I attempt to go round in time

indicators.note: the attempt word goes round the other pieces, enclosing them

parts.note: to try is to attempt
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A traveller attempts to fit a round of places into the time available.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go round' tells the attempt word to enclose the phrase 'in time', read as two pieces rather than a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An itinerary is a planned route, a list of places to be visited on a journey.

clue.text: Write following round in golf contest

indicators.note: the write word follows the round letter

parts.note: O is round in shape
to pen is to write

explanation.surface: Someone writes up a round at a golf tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf an open is a tournament anyone qualified may enter, like the British Open.
explanation.definitionFit: An open is a golf tournament open to amateurs and professionals alike.

clue.text: A measure of sound character in the Bible

parts.note: the bel is a unit of sound intensity, ten decibels

explanation.surface: A sound-measuring character appears in scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel, second son of Adam and Eve, is killed by Cain in Genesis.

clue.text: Source of fruit, black, found on walk

parts.note: B is short for black, as on pencils
a ramble is a leisurely walk

explanation.surface: Blackberries are found while out on a country walk.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'found on' puts B above RAMBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The bramble is the blackberry bush, which bears the fruit.

clue.text: I'm attending G&S piece, wanting it to start soon?

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped
Patience is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera

explanation.surface: A theatregoer at a Gilbert and Sullivan show wants it to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attending' is a link joining I'M to PATIENCE, the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta. The surface wants the opera to start; the definition is eagerness.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanting something to begin without delay is restless eagerness, the lack of tolerance for waiting.

clue.text: Stone peak accommodating dreadful climbing

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means read upwards, backwards
the peak word houses the other inside it

parts.note: the top is the peak
dire means dreadful

explanation.surface: A climber dreads a stony peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accommodating' puts dreadful inside peak, making TODIREP, and 'climbing' turns that upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Peridot is a green gemstone, a variety of olivine, so a precious stone.

clue.text: Looking embarrassed as study oversteps limits

indicators.note: the study word steps over the limits word, straddling it

parts.note: to con is to study, an old sense
rims are edges, limits

explanation.surface: A student blushes on going too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oversteps' has the study word straddle the limits word; 'con' meaning study is an old sense. 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Crimson is a deep red, the colour of a face flushing in embarrassment.

clue.text: Presumably not a painter of seascapes?

definitions.text: Presumably not a painter of seascapes?

parts.words: Presumably not a painter of seascapes?
parts.note: split the painter's name into two words meaning one who looks at the land, not the sea

explanation.surface: A guess about which artist never painted the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edwin Landseer was a Victorian painter of animals, best known for 'The Monarch of the Glen' and the Trafalgar Square lions.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edwin Landseer, the Victorian animal painter, whose name splits into land plus seer.

clue.text: Councillor is repeatedly in a difficult situation

indicators.note: repeatedly means the word is given twice

explanation.surface: A councillor keeps getting into a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is a time of acute difficulty, a difficult situation.

clue.text: Freight vehicle supplied with energy

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
go means energy, vigour

explanation.surface: A freight vehicle has been fuelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supplied with' is a link joining the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo is the goods carried by a ship or plane, its freight.

clue.text: Back-up system offered by tailors?

parts.note: two ways of holding trousers up at once, sold by clothiers, as an idiom for doubled safety measures

explanation.surface: A tailor offers a spare system.
explanation.walkthrough: Wearing both a belt and braces (US suspenders) is the British idiom for taking double precautions.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for taking two precautions where one would do, from wearing both trouser supports.

clue.text: Someone appearing in the Bible a good deal

explanation.surface: A biblical figure gets a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham's nephew in Genesis shares a name with the word for a large quantity.

clue.text: Guard dispatched by railway

parts.note: sent means dispatched

explanation.surface: A guard is sent away by train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry is a soldier posted to keep guard.

clue.text: Worthless pony went for a Burton

indicators.note: British slang: gone for a Burton means wrecked, so the letters are broken up

explanation.surface: A worthless pony has been lost.
explanation.walkthrough: PONY and WENT are scrambled; 'went for a Burton' (RAF slang for killed or ruined) reads as the surface verb, but only 'for a Burton' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Twopenny means costing twopence, hence cheap and of little worth.
